paper_title: LayoutRecall: Preserving Appearance in Multi-Round 3D Layout-Controlled Image Editing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 3D layout-controlled image editing gives users explicit control over object placement and camera viewpoint. In a sequence of edits, however, the latest image can lose the appearance of an object when it is occluded or leaves view. The target layout specifies where the object should reappear, while its appearance must be recovered from earlier observations. We introduce LayoutRecall, a multi-round editor that stores and reuses appearance in the local coordinate systems of 3D boxes. Box-Surface Latent Memory retains image latents on box faces and retrieves them along rays in the target view. Geometry-Aligned Memory Conditioning supplies the retrieved tokens to a FLUX.2 editor using target-view positions, shared box-local embeddings, and object-wise attention. A correspondence loss encourages the editor to attend to matching observations during denoising. We also introduce LayoutLoop, a multi-round 3D layout-controlled image editing benchmark with calibrated layouts and designed revisits. We conduct extensive experiments on LayoutLoop and real-scene data to verify the ability of our method. The project page is at https://ykchizs.github.io/layoutrecall.github.io/.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: LayoutRecall: Preserving Appearance in Multi-Round 3D Layout-Controlled Image Editing Yankuan Chi1 Xin Lin1 Baihan Yang1 Yuheng Liu2 1University of California San Diego Jason Li3 2University of California Irvine Truong Nguyen1 3Nanyang Technological University Figure 1. Multi-round 3D layout-controlled image editing with LayoutRecall. The user specifies the layout of the objects with 3D boxes (top) and edits the image (bottom) by adding, moving, or deleting an object box or changing the camera view in each round. LayoutRecall preserves appearance when an object reappears in later round (toy car, yellow circle).

sections.content: 3D layout-controlled image editing gives users explicit control over object placement and camera viewpoint. Introduction 3D layout-controlled generation and editing allow users to compose scene by specifying object positions, orientations, and sizes with 3D boxes and adjusting the camera viewpoint [1, 5, 19, 32, 42, 51]. This interface supports object addition, movement, and deletion with coarse geometry, making it useful for product visualization, scene design, and data generation for perception [10]. In practice, users refine scenes through successive edits, requiring precise spatial control and stable appearance. Existing layout-conditioned editors control individual transformations from source image [5, 51]. Reusing only the latest output loses evidence about objects that become occluded or leave view. subsequent layout may bring an object back at different position, but the box describes its geometry and leaves its original appearance underdeter1 mined. The editor can therefore satisfy the requested placement while generating different instance. This failure differs from the gradual image degradation observed in recursive editing [26, 58, 68]. It also affects background regions exposed after an occluder moves away. Recovery requires retaining earlier observations and aligning them with the target after objects and cameras move. We build LayoutRecall on the observation that 3D box provides both spatial control signal and coordinate system that moves with the object. Box-Surface Latent Memory (BSLM) uses this coordinate system to retain observed appearance on the box surface and retrieve it through rays from the target view. This operation transfers stored observation to the corresponding location in the requested layout. Geometry-Aligned Memory Conditioning (GAMC) then places the retrieved latents in the target image, embeds their box-local surface coordinates, and restricts attention to the appropriate object region. Correspondence Attention Loss (CAL) trains the FLUX.2 editor to use matching observations during denoising. Repeated reading and writing carries appearance forward through successive changes in layout and visibility  (Fig. 1)  . We introduce LayoutLoop to evaluate this capability on calibrated multiview sequences with object revisits and camera returns. ten-round rollout measures image quality, editing accuracy, preservation, and consistency across editing rounds. We conduct extensive experiments on LayoutLoop and real-scene data to evaluate these aspects. Our contributions are as follows. We develop LayoutRecall for multi-round 3D layoutcontrolled image editing, covering object addition, movement, deletion, and camera view change. We introduce BSLM and GAMC to store and retrieve appearance in object-local coordinates and guide denoising with spatial and semantic correspondences. CAL supervises attention to matching observations. We construct LayoutLoop, calibrated multiview dataset and benchmark that uses revisits to test the overall image quality, editing accuracy, appearance preservation, and camera-return consistency. 2. Related Work 3D layout control. Spatial conditions provide means to control scene geometry in image synthesis and editing. Depth maps constrain dense scene structure [6, 19], while orientation and occlusion cues target specific relations [16, 25, 31, 35, 39, 40, 64]. Another line of work utilizes explicit 3D representations as conditions, but at the cost of high computational demand and imperfect reconstruction [15, 38, 52, 56, 59, 62]. Three-dimensional boxes offer explicit object-level control. Neural Assets [55] and LACONIC [32] encode box parameters as tokens, and other approaches use boxes to guide object inpainting [10, 36]. SceneCraft [60], SceneDesigner [42], SeeThrough3D [1], and Mise-en-Video [72] condition generation on projected layouts. BoxCtrl [51] and Thinking-in-Boxes [5] adapt related spatial interfaces to single-round image editing. Our work uses projected layouts to specify each edit and the underlying boxes to associate appearance across rounds. Multi-turn editing. Repeated edits accumulate errors as each generated output becomes the next input. Trainingbased methods adapt editors to imperfect inputs [12, 17, 21, 43, 46, 61, 68]. Inference-time methods change frequency content, sampling, or model components to improve stability [3, 22, 26, 53, 71]. The above methods all focus on holistic image quality instead of each entitys appearance. Agents and history-based approaches can also condition on earlier turns [13, 41, 45, 58]. We study complementary recovery problem in which spatial edit removes visual evidence from the current frame and later edit makes that content visible again. The target geometry provides way to locate the relevant observations in the new view. Appearance memory for generation. Long video generators retain earlier observations through frame context, compressed history, or spatial retrieval [49, 54, 63, 66, 69]. Entity-centric memories organize past appearances into slots or object groups [14, 18, 23, 28, 30, 57, 65, 70]. For explicit layout edits, an objects identity determines which history to retrieve, and its new box pose determines where that history should appear. BSLM addresses observations by both object identity and box-surface position. GAMC uses those addresses to place observations in the target view and condition the appropriate object regions. 3. Geometry-Aligned Memory Conditioning The retrieval step identifies appearance evidence for the requested scene geometry. GAMC supplies that evidence to the editor with its target image position, object-local surface coordinate, and object identity. These three signals locate the observation in the output, indicate which surface it describes, and determine which object can access it. Target-view token placement. We fine-tune the [7] editor with FLUX.2 operation-specific LoRA adapters [20]. The VAE encodes It1, Bt1, and Bt as clean reference tokens, which are appended to the noisy target tokens. Distinct time-axis offsets in RoPE [48] identify the three reference streams (10, 20, and 30). We append retrieved memory tokens as fourth stream at offset 40. Its spatial RoPE indices are the projected locations in the target image, so the positional encoding follows the requested placement and viewpoint. Box-local Fourier embedding. Target image coordinates place memory token in the output image plane. To encode its box surface correspondence across views, we also provide the box-local surface coordinate of the memory token, following the use of local box coordinates in SceneDesigner [42]. Our later experiments show that the model trained on two-edit sequences can be directly applied to long editing sequences. 4. Experiments We evaluate LayoutRecall on singleand multi-round 3D layout-controlled editing. Single-round comparisons measure spatial control and preservation. Multi-round comparisons and ablations assess how memory and box-local correspondence support consistency. 4.1. Proposed Dataset We introduce LayoutLoop, multiview dataset for 3D layout-controlled image editing. It provides training set of two-edit revisit sequences and an evaluation benchmark of single-round edits and ten-round editing sequences. Existing rendered editing datasets provide image pairs for individual 3D edits [5, 33, 51], and multi-round datasets cover sequences of object transformations [47] or generated editing trajectories [13]. In contrast, LayoutLoop pairs multiview renders with calibrated 3D layouts across object addition, movement, deletion, and camera changes, and includes revisits in scenes with detailed backgrounds. Scene and state construction. Each arrangement places two to five BlenderKit assets in an artist-made BlenderKit scene [9], subject to the available placement area. An arrangement has base state and up to three edited states: the added state inserts an object, the moved state translates and rotates an existing object, and the offset state moves the same object by 0.22 on the ground plane and rotates it by at most 45. We check placements against rendered scene geometry and flag remaining visible intersections. Shared cameras and annotations. We sample up to 16 views on an arc facing the arrangement, prioritizing views in which the added object and at least one pose of the moved object are visible. The offset pose is chosen so that the object remains visible in most of these views. All states are rendered with Blender EEVEE [8] under the scene lighting, and sharing cameras across states yields aligned observations of each edit. Each render includes 3D boxes, camera parameters, and instance masks. Qwen3-VL [4] generates asset categories and captions. Revisit sequences. Transitions between the base and added states yield addition and deletion edits, transitions among the base, moved, and offset states yield object movements, and changes of view yield camera edits. Chaining these transitions produces both exact returns and revisits at an offset pose or nearby view. In total, LayoutLoop contains 498 arrangements in 164 scenes, with 247 distinct assets, 6,954 views, and 25,964 renders. 4.2. Experimental Setup Evaluation sequences. For synthetic evaluation, we use LayoutLoop (Sec. 4.1): 400 single-round edits (100 per operation) and 50 ten-round sequences that mix addition, movement, deletion, and camera changes and revisit objects and views after intervening edits. For real-scene evaluation, we select COCO images [27] in which every major object has matching WildDet3D 3D box annotation [2], yielding 80 single-round edits (20 per operation) and 10 ten-round sequences. Compared methods. We compare with SeeThrough3D [1], 3D layout-conditioned generator, and with BoxCtrl [51] and Thinking-in-Boxes [5], two single-round 3D layoutcontrolled editors, in both single-round and multi-round editing. All three receive the same underlying geometry in their respective layout formats; SeeThrough3D generates from the target layout alone, whereas the two editors also condition on the current image. In multiround editing, every method runs recursively on its own outputs. Metrics. On LayoutLoop, image quality is measured by MUSIQ, the mean absolute difference between the MUSIQ scores [24] of each output and its reference render. Single-round editing accuracy is measured per operation: CLIP-T [44] for addition, DINOv2 [37] similarity between source and target crops for movement, DINOv2 similarity between the output and the reference within the projected box of the removed object for deletion, and full-image DINOv2 similarity to the reference for camera changes. Preservation is measured by PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [67] outside the edited regions. Grounding DINO [29] detections provide the mIoU with the projected target boxes and the edit success rate. For consistency, Back computes PSNR when the camera returns to an earlier view, and Self computes the DINOv2 similarity between an object and the models first observation of the same object. Since real scenes have no edited references, we use only reference-free metrics on them. Preservation compares each output with the methods own source image outside the boxes of the edited object, and Back compares camera return with the methods own earlier output at that view, outside all boxes. Survive is the fraction of unedited and visible objects that Grounding DINO still detects inside their boxes after the edit. MUSIQ is measured against the input photograph instead of reference render; lower values indicate that the editor better retains the photographic quality of the input. Implementation. We build on FLUX.2-klein-9B-base with rank-16 LoRA (α = 32). Each operation-specific adapter is trained on 20k sequences with learning rate of 104 and 10 gradient accumulation steps. The retrieved memory is capped at 2048 tokens per round. We set the object assignment threshold to τobj = 20%, the matching radius to ρ = 1.5 token footprints, the correspondence loss weight to λ = 0.025, and the memory dropout probability to = 0.15. The training of LoRA checkpoint takes 15 hours on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, and an editing round at inference takes 24 seconds. 4.3. On LayoutLoop, it achieves the best image quality, the best preservation, and the highest movement, deletion, and camera accuracy. Figure 5 shows consistent appearance when objects reappear (yellow circles). 4.5. Ablation Study We compare the full model with three variants: without BLC-Fourier, with memory from only the last two frames, and without memory. Results are shown in Tabs. 5 and 6 and Fig. 6. Removing the memory causes substantial drops in image quality, preservation, and consistency. Keeping memory from only the last two frames yields scores between those of the memory-free variant and the full model, as expected. These results confirm the importance of long-term memory for maintaining consistency over long editing sequences. Removing BLC-Fourier moderately reduces most scores and can distort objects  (Fig. 6)  , supporting its role in establishing spatial correspondence. 5. Conclusion LayoutRecall extends 3D layout-controlled image editing to sequences that revisit earlier objects and views. BSLM stores historical appearance in box-local surface coordinates, and GAMC conditions the editing on observations projected into the requested scene with spatial and semantic alignments. CAL encourages the editor to use the matching surface evidence. Through extensive experiments, we show that our model preserves object appearance more effectively than other models and ablation variants with shorter or empty memory, while retaining the ability to produce highquality outputs and follow spatial edits precisely. Figure 4. Qualitative results of single-round editing. The prompts for the two added objects are an orange traffic cone and stack of wooden pallets. tion scores. Qualitative results are shown in Fig. 4. Overall, adding the memory module does not compromise singleround editing: LayoutRecall performs on par with or better than methods designed specifically for this setting. We attribute this to dataset fine-tuning and memory dropout. 4.4. Multi-Round Editing Tables 3 and 4 report multi-round results. LayoutRecall achieves the best results on most metrics. On LayoutLoop, SeeThrough3D obtains higher editing accuracy at the cost of very low preservation. On real scenes, BoxCtrl replaces each scene with an empty background in the first round, which inflates its PSNR and Back scores, but leads to by far the worst MUSIQ. Without access to 3D layout information, the general multi-turn editors (MT-OPSD and FreqEdit) rarely follow the editing instructions or produce the intended scene, resulting in very low editing accuracy. The single-round 3D layout-controlled methods obtain low preservation and consistency scores, since they retain no information about objects from previous rounds. In contrast, LayoutRecall executes the editing instructions precisely and maintains consistency throughout the editing process. Moreover, because the appearance stored in memory is injected at every round, LayoutRecall is less susceptible to image quality degradation and achieves high overall 7 Figure 5. Qualitative results of multi-round editing. SeeThrough3D regenerates the target while completely discarding the original content. BoxCtrl replaces the scene with an empty background. With its long-term memory, LayoutRecall restores the toy car previously hidden by the moved sofa in round 7 and the plant previously hidden by the added cabinet in round 8 (yellow circles). Figure 6. Qualitative ablation results. When the camera returns in round 3, only the full model restores the orange ball (yellow circle). Without BLC-Fourier, the stone table and the bike are distorted. 8 Limitations. The box surface approximates object geometry, so neighboring-cell retrieval can introduce appearance in empty parts of loose box. Also, background recovery depends on previously observed camera views.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: This supplementary material provides the implementation details of LayoutRecall (Sec. A), the full evaluation protocol (Sec. B), additional qualitative results of multiround editing (Sec. C), an analysis of image degradation over long editing sequences (Sec. D), and the details of our dataset LayoutLoop (Sec. E). A. Implementation Details Backbone and inputs. LayoutRecall builds on FLUX.2klein-9B-base [7], flow-matching transformer with 8 double-stream blocks, 24 single-stream blocks, and hidden size of 4096. The FLUX.2 VAE encodes each 16 16 image patch into one token with 128 channels. The text prompt is the short caption of the new object for addition and fixed prompt for the other operations. In each round, the transformer jointly attends to the text tokens, the noisy target tokens, the reference streams Bt1, Bt, and It1 (with RoPE time offsets of 10, 20, and 30), and the retrieved memory tokens (offset 40). Operation-specific models. Each operation has its own LoRA adapter (rank 16, α = 32) on the attention projections and MLPs of all transformer blocks, together with its own BLC-Fourier MLP and background embedding. Since addition introduces new object without any stored appearance, it uses the single-round adapter without memory, whereas deletion, movement, and camera changes use the memory adapters. Table 7 summarizes the hyperparameters. Memory writing. SAM 3 receives the category and caption of each object as text prompts. An instance is accepted as the object mask if its score is at least 0.3 and at least 60% of its pixels lie inside the projected box; weaker instance with score of at least 0.02 is accepted if at least 90% of its pixels lie inside the box. An object more than half covered by the boxes of other objects is treated as hidden and is not written. Masks are clipped to the projected boxes, and pixel claimed by several objects is assigned to the box that is nearest along its ray. For each token assigned to an object, we intersect the camera ray through the token center with the box of that object. If several tokens hit the same cell, the token nearest to the cell center is written. stored cell is replaced only by an observation whose projected area is at least 1.25 larger, i.e., an observation at higher image resolution. Deleting an object also removes its memory. Background tokens not covered by any mask or box are stored once per camera view and image location. Memory retrieval. The ray of each target token is interTable 7. Hyperparameters of LayoutRecall. Box-Surface Latent Memory Cell size Object token threshold τobj Replacement margin Memory budget Instance masks (SAM 3 [11]) Text prompts Accepted instance Weak instance Hidden object 8 cm on each box face 20% mask coverage 1.25 projected area 1024 (training), 2048 (inference) category and short caption score 0.3, 60% inside box score 0.02, 90% inside box > 50% of box behind other boxes Geometry-Aligned Memory Conditioning BLC-Fourier Object attention region Background attention region Training Steps Batch Optimizer Schedule Timesteps Loss weight of edited region Memory dropout CAL Inference Sampling zero39 1024 4096, initialized output box coverage 5%, dilated by 1 token box coverage < 50%, dilated by 1 token 20k sequences 1, 10 gradient accumulation steps AdamW, lr 104, weight decay 0.01 cosine, 50 warm-up updates U[0, 1] 5 0.15 λ = 0.025, β = 0.3, ρ = 1.5 tokens, 8 double blocks first 8 heads 50 steps, no classifier-free guidance sected with the front-most target box. If the hit cell is stored, it is used directly; otherwise, with lookup radius of 1, we use the nearest stored cell within one cell on the same face. Each retrieved cell contributes one memory token, positioned at the projection of its cell center under the target box and camera. Background memory is retrieved from the target camera view if that view has been observed. If the target view is that of It1, we retrieve the stored background tokens that were covered by the boxes in It1 and are visible in the target. When the retrieved tokens exceed the memory budget, high-frequency tokens are kept first. Warped background. For an unobserved camera view, the 12 camera model warps the stored views into the target view, using ground plane at the lowest box bottom and backdrop sphere around the scene. warped token is kept if at least 90% of its pixels are valid and its reprojection error, estimated by varying the sphere radius and the ground height, is at most one token. The warped composite is encoded by the VAE and receives separate learned background embedding. Training. Each LoRA checkpoint is trained on 20k twoedit sequences (I0, I1, I2). The ground-truth frames I0 and I1 are written into memory, and the loss is computed only on the second edit. The memory stream is dropped with probability = 0.15. The base model, VAE, text encoder, and SAM 3 remain frozen. Training one memory adapter takes 15 hours on single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. Inference. Inference is recursive: each round takes the previous output of the model as It1, the masks of generated frames are computed online with SAM 3, and each generated frame is written into memory at the end of its round. One editing round takes 24 seconds. B. Evaluation Protocol B.1. Synthetic Scenes Projected regions. We project the eight corners of box through the camera and clip their bounding rectangle to the image. For object-level metrics, this crop is padded to square and resized to 224 224. When the camera is fixed, we identify the edited pixels from the RGB difference between the source and target reference renders and dilate the resulting mask by 8 pixels: Table 8. Per-operation editing accuracy on LayoutLoop. Consistency. An object is considered visible when at least half of its pixels are visible according to the reference instance masks. Back is the PSNR at rounds that return to an earlier camera view, computed against the reference render before the camera change and excluding the projected boxes of objects edited in between. Self is the DINOv2 cosine similarity between the crop of each visible object and its crop at its first visible observation in the outputs of the same method, averaged over objects and rounds. Image quality. We compute MUSIQ [24] (trained on KonIQ-10k) for every output and its reference render at MUSIQ is the absolute difthe evaluation resolution. ference between the two scores, averaged over all outputs of method. Unlike the raw score, the absolute difference penalizes deviations in either direction: degradation lowers MUSIQ, whereas global brightening or regenerating the scene can raise it without preserving the input. The mask thus also covers secondary effects such as shadows and reflections, and preservation (PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [67]) is measured on its complement. In single-round editing, preservation is computed for addition, deletion, and movement; camera changes are excluded because they alter the whole image. Per-operation editing accuracy. Table 8 defines the peroperation editing accuracy metrics. Detection-based editing accuracy. We query Grounding DINO [29] with the object category, using box and text thresholds of 0.3 and 0.25. For addition and movement, we take the maximum IoU between any detection and the projected target box. For camera change, we average these per-object maxima over all visible objects. The mIoU is averaged over addition, movement, and camera changes, and each of these edits counts as success when its IoU exceeds 0.5. deletion succeeds when every detection of the Evaluation data. We start from the COCO [27] images annotated with 3D boxes in WildDet3D [2]. An image is candidate if it has at most 10 valid 3D boxes and every COCO object covering at least 1% of the image is matched by 3D box whose projection has an IoU of at least 0.5 with the COCO box. Among the candidates with 310 boxes inside the central square crop, we select 20 images by visual inspection, requiring visible ground plane, tight boxes, and box for every major object, and we remove duplicate boxes. Each image is center-cropped to square. The boxes are converted to gravity-aligned boxes on common ground plane whose up direction is the mean vertical axis of the boxes, and each scene is uniformly rescaled to typical object heights, which leaves all projections unchanged. The converted boxes reproject within median of 5 pixels of the original annotations. Edits are generated automatically: deleting visible object, moving standing object by 0.81.8 times its size, adding one of eight everyday objects next to an existing object, and orbiting the camera by 10 13 18. Every edit is checked to stay in view and to be free of collisions. Reference-free metrics. Since real scenes have no reference renders of the edited states, we use reference-free metrics. Preservation compares each output with the source image of the same method, excluding the boxes of the edited object in both frames, dilated by 8 pixels. Back compares an output at revisited camera view with the earlier output of the same method at that view, excluding all boxes in both frames. Survive is the fraction of unedited, visible objects that Grounding DINO still detects inside their target boxes (IoU above 0.5) after the edit. Detection-based accuracy and Self follow the synthetic protocol, and MUSIQ is measured against the input photograph. C. Additional Qualitative Results Figure 7 shows an additional multi-round editing sequence. The camera orbit in round 1 hides the orange ball behind the car and moves the tree and the streetlight out of view, and moving the car back in round 9 hides the rock. LayoutRecall restores the ball, the tree, and the streetlight when the camera returns in round 3, and the rock when the car is deleted in round 10, while the background and the remaining objects stay consistent throughout the sequence. D. Image Degradation over Long Editing Sequences major challenge in multi-round image editing is error accumulation. Because each round operates on the output of the previous one, small artifacts accumulate over long editing sequence and eventually degrade the image. We examine this effect for different methods. Results. We run LayoutRecall, Thinking-in-Boxes [5], MTOPSD [68], and FreqEdit [26] for 50 rounds and show the results in Fig. 8. All methods accumulate errors and degrade as the number of rounds increases, but the outputs of LayoutRecall remain the cleanest. Memory as high-quality anchor. We attribute this robustness to the memory design. Without memory, an editor conditions only on its previous output, so an artifact, once it appears, is propagated and amplified in every later round. In LayoutRecall, the tokens retrieved from BSLM enter the denoising process of every round as clean references for the visible objects and the background, so the generation is guided by the stored appearance in addition to the possibly degraded previous output. Moreover, BSLM keeps only high-resolution observations: stored token is replaced only by an observation of the same surface cell at substantially higher image resolution (Tab. 7), and background tokens are written once per view and image location. Later observations at the same or coarser resolution, including degraded ones, therefore never overwrite the stored appearance, which typically comes from the input image or the sharpest earlier view. The memory tokens thus act as high-quality anchor that pulls each round back toward the established appearance and alleviates error accumulation over long sequences. E. Placement. We place objects from the longest footprint side to the shortest, at random points of the region and with yaw drawn uniformly from [180, 180]. first-pass pose is accepted when camera-ray samples of the region support its footprint, and its footprint, padded by 3.5 cm, and its axis-aligned box overlap those of the other objects by at most 1.5 cm. The moved state re-draws the pose of one object at least max(min(0.6 d, 0.25 w), 0.15 m) from its base position, where is the longer footprint side. The added state places one further object against the base layout. We then audit the base, moved and added states of every arrangement for visible interpenetration with rigid scene geometry, which flags 254 of the 498 arrangements at 1 cm or more. We regenerate flagged arrangements where possible: 206 are regenerated, 48 remain flagged, and the other 244 keep their first-pass layout. regenerated pose must also have rendered support under its footprint, with gap of at most 0.3 m, and pass collision test. This test uses the scene geometry as rendered, including instances and render-time displacement. It rejects crossings of rigid geometry more than 1 cm above the bottom of the object (up to 15 cm for small instanced ground cover), containment in either direction and overlap with placed objects; vegetation crossings are recorded but not rejected. Perspective views use 35 mm lens on 36 mm sensor, except for one scene keyframed to 24 mm and two with other sensors, and 13 scenes keep lens shift. Six scenes keep an orthographic camera, and three keep panoramic setting that EEVEE renders as pinhole. Offset state. To fill the distance bins evenly, feasibility search tests every arrangement in each 0.2 bin, with directions every 15 and radii across the bin. We assign arrangements to bins, most constrained first, into the bin with the largest deficit, and draw the turn uniformly from [45, 45].
